title: Differencing a trend away
objectives: Difference a series to make it stationary.
Choose between differencing and detrending, and find the order of integration with a test.

screens.title: A trend and its changes
screens.prose: Top: a seeded random walk with drift, $x_t = x_{t-1} + \mu + \varepsilon_t$, over 500 days. Bottom: its daily change, $x_t - x_{t-1}$. Slide the drift $\mu$ from 0 to 0.4.

derive.caption: Drift {{drift}} a day: the change averages {{drift}}

screens.question: As the drift grows, what happens to the bottom panel?

options.text: It moves up to sit around $\mu$, and still has no trend
It starts to trend upwards too
options.why: Slide to 0.4 and look again. The changes sit higher, around 0.4, but their level never climbs.

options.text: Nothing at all changes
options.why: Watch the bottom panel's centre as you slide: it rises from 0 to 0.4.

options.text: Its swings get wider
options.why: The swings come from $\varepsilon_t$, which does not change. Only the centre moves.

hints.text: Slide from 0 to 0.4 and watch the centre of the bottom panel.
The bottom series is $\mu + \varepsilon_t$.
The top climbs faster; the bottom shifts up to a new constant level.

feedback.correct: Correct. Differencing turns a drift into a constant mean.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the bottom panel at drift 0 and drift 0.4.

explain.text: $x_t - x_{t-1} = \mu + \varepsilon_t$ is noise around a constant, so the trend in the top panel becomes a mean in the bottom one. A constant mean is allowed in a stationary series. With $\mu = 0$ the change is pure white noise.

screens.title: Differencing
screens.prose: The **first difference** is $\Delta x_t = x_t - x_{t-1}$; the second is $\Delta^2 x_t = \Delta x_t - \Delta x_{t-1}$. A series that becomes stationary after $d$ differences, and not before, is **integrated of order $d$**, written I($d$). The walk is I(1).

state.caption: Squares: two differences leave a constant.

screens.question: Complete `difference(x, d)`: apply the first difference $d$ times.

widget.how: Check runs 7 hidden tests: squares and cubes differenced 1 to 3 times, $d = 0$, lengths, and a seeded walk whose difference must give back its shocks exactly. The first run loads NumPy, which takes a few seconds.

hints.text: Each pass is the lag-1 subtraction from lesson 1.
Each pass makes the array one shorter.

feedback.correct: Correct. Differencing the seeded walk gave back its 499 shocks exactly.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Each pass subtracts yesterday from today: `y[1:] - y[:-1]`.

explain.text: A walk is the running sum of its shocks, so one difference undoes the sum and returns the shocks. $d$ passes lose $d$ values from the front. `np.diff(x, n=d)` does the same in one call.

screens.title: How many differences?
screens.prose: Three seeded series of 500 days, rescaled to fit one chart. One is stationary, one is a walk, and one is the running sum of a walk: its slope itself wanders.
screens.question: Match each series to the differences it needs.

hints.text: Which series is smooth like a curve, which jagged but wandering, which jagged around a fixed level?
P bends smoothly: its slope changes slowly.
Q stays put: I(0). R wanders with jagged steps: I(1). P is smooth and curving, because each day adds a walk to it: I(2).

feedback.correct: Correct. Q needs none, R one, and P two.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A walk is jagged; the sum of a walk is smooth, because its steps change slowly.

byKey.d2: Look at P again: it curves smoothly. Its daily change is itself a walk, so it needs two differences.
byKey.d1: R is jagged and wanders with no pull back: one difference makes it noise.
byKey.d0: Q keeps returning to one level: it is already stationary.

explain.text: Differencing P once gives a walk, the slope that wanders; differencing again gives noise. In finance, prices are close to I(1). I(2) series are rare, though some price indices behave that way.

screens.title: Finding $d$ with a test
screens.prose: Automate the count: run the ADF test (lesson 3), and while it fails to reject a unit root, difference once more. Stop at the first $d$ that rejects, or give up after `max_d`.
screens.question: Complete `integration_order(x, max_d, alpha)`.

widget.starter:
import numpy as np
from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import adfuller

def integration_order(x, max_d, alpha):
    y = np.asarray(x, dtype=float)
    for d in range(max_d + 1):
        if ...:                  # ADF p-value of y below alpha
            return d
        y = ...                  # difference once more
    return None
widget.how: Check runs 7 hidden tests on seeded series: noise, walks with and without drift, a summed walk, an AR(1) and a straight trend plus noise. Each must return the expected $d$, or None. The first run loads statsmodels with NumPy, SciPy and pandas, which takes 20 to 40 seconds; later runs are quick.

hints.text: `adfuller(y, autolag="AIC")[1]` is the p-value.
The walk rejects only after one difference.
The condition is `adfuller(y, autolag="AIC")[1] < alpha`, and the update is `y = np.diff(y)`.

feedback.correct: Correct. Note the last test: a straight trend plus noise came out as $d = 1$.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Test first, then difference, and return the first $d$ that rejects.

explain.text: The trend plus noise was given $d = 1$, because the default test has a constant but no trend. Its difference is stationary, but it is not the right fix: the next two screens show why.

screens.title: Differencing a straight trend
screens.prose: A different trend: $x_t = 0.05\,t + \varepsilon_t$, a straight line plus noise. It always returns to its line. Bottom: its first difference, $0.05 + \varepsilon_t - \varepsilon_{t-1}$.
screens.question: What does differencing do to this series?

options.text: It makes it stationary, but doubles the noise variance and adds a negative lag-1 correlation
Exactly what it does to a walk: it returns the shocks
options.why: Here each change holds two shocks, $\varepsilon_t - \varepsilon_{t-1}$, not one. The walk's change holds one.

options.text: Nothing: the difference is still not stationary
options.why: It is stationary: noise around 0.05. The problem is what the extra shock costs.

options.text: It keeps the trend
options.why: The trend became the constant 0.05, as with the drift on the first screen.

hints.text: Write out $x_t - x_{t-1}$ term by term.
Each change contains today's shock and minus yesterday's.
$\text{Var}(\varepsilon_t - \varepsilon_{t-1}) = 2\sigma^2$, and neighbouring changes share a shock with opposite signs.

feedback.correct: Correct. The sample variance is 2.02, against 1 for the noise, and the lag-1 correlation is −0.49.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write the difference as $0.05 + \varepsilon_t - \varepsilon_{t-1}$ and look at what it contains.

explain.text: The difference is an MA(1) with a unit root in its MA part: a lag-1 correlation of −0.5 in theory, −0.49 here. That is **over-differencing**: the series becomes harder to forecast and its noise doubles. Subtracting the fitted line would have left plain noise.

screens.title: Detrending
screens.prose: The alternative to differencing: fit a straight line $a + bt$ by least squares and keep the residuals, $x_t - (a + bt)$. For the straight trend plus noise this gives back the noise, without the extra shock.

state.caption: A perfect line leaves zero residuals.

screens.question: Complete `detrend_linear(x)`: return the residuals from a fitted straight line in time.

widget.starter:
import numpy as np

def detrend_linear(x):
    x = np.asarray(x, dtype=float)
    t = np.arange(len(x))
    b, a = np.polyfit(t, x, 1)     # slope, then intercept
    return ...                     # x minus the fitted line
widget.how: Check runs 6 hidden tests: a straight line (residuals all 0), a short list, the length, and seeded series, rounded to 6 places. The first run loads NumPy, which takes a few seconds.

hints.text: `np.polyfit(t, x, 1)` returns the slope first, then the intercept.
The fitted value at time $t$ is `a + b * t`.
`return x - (a + b * t)`.

feedback.correct: Correct. The residuals of a least-squares line always average 0.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Subtract `a + b * t` from `x`.

explain.text: On the trend plus noise the residuals have sd close to 1, the noise itself: no information lost and none added. Whether to detrend or difference depends on the kind of trend, which the next two screens settle.

screens.title: Detrending a walk
screens.prose: An analyst fits a straight line to a seeded random walk (top) and keeps the residuals (bottom). "The trend is gone, so the residual is stationary." An ADF test on the residual gives p = 0.46.
screens.question: What is wrong with the claim?

options.text: A walk has no line to return to: the residual still wanders, so it still has a unit root
Nothing: removing the line makes any series stationary
options.why: You treated the fitted line as the trend. A walk's wandering is not a line, and the residual's ADF p is 0.46.

options.text: The analyst should fit a curve instead
options.why: Any curve fitted to one walk will chase its wiggles in-sample and fail out of sample. A walk needs differencing.

options.text: The residual has mean 0, which proves it is stationary
options.why: Least-squares residuals always average 0. That says nothing about whether they wander.

hints.text: Does the bottom series keep crossing 0?
Look at how long the residual stays on one side of 0.
It stays above or below 0 for long stretches, as the walk does. Fitting a line removed the average slope, not the wandering.

feedback.correct: Correct. A stochastic trend cannot be subtracted away; it has to be differenced.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether the residual behaves any differently from the walk.

byKey.true: You treated detrending as a cure for any trend. It removes a fixed line; a walk's trend is the sum of its shocks.
byKey.mean: Zero mean holds by construction for any least-squares residual.

explain.text: The residual of a detrended walk still wanders: here it starts at −14.8 and the test fails to reject (p = 0.46). Worse, a regression on time usually looks significant for a walk, the spurious trend of Markov Chains, lesson 12. Difference a stochastic trend; detrend a deterministic one.

screens.title: Difference or detrend?
screens.prose: The ADF test with a trend term, `regression="ct"`, has $H_0$: a unit root, possibly with drift, against stationary around a straight line. The table runs both versions on the walk and on the straight trend plus noise.
screens.question: What should you do to each?

options.text: Difference the walk; detrend the trend plus noise
Difference both
options.why: With the trend term the second series rejects a unit root at any level: it is stationary around a line. Differencing it over-differences.

options.text: Detrend both
options.why: The walk fails to reject even with a trend term (p = 0.77). Detrending leaves its unit root in place, as the trap showed.

options.text: Detrend the walk; difference the trend plus noise
options.why: That is the swap of both mistakes: a residual that still wanders, and a difference with doubled noise.

hints.text: Read the "ct" column.
The trend plus noise rejects with the trend term.
Rejecting with "ct" means stationary around a line: detrend. Not rejecting means a stochastic trend: difference.

feedback.correct: Correct. The trend term decides between a stochastic and a deterministic trend.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A rejection with the trend term means the series returns to a line.

explain.text: With only a constant the trend plus noise looks like a walk (p = 0.97), because a constant cannot describe a line. With the trend term it rejects (p = 0.0000). The walk fails both, so it has a stochastic trend and needs differencing.

screens.title: A weekly pattern
screens.prose: Seeded daily volume for a share, in millions, over 60 weeks: busy on Mondays and Fridays, quiet midweek. Its mean depends on the weekday, so it is not stationary. The **seasonal difference** $x_t - x_{t-5}$ compares each day with the same weekday a week before.
screens.question: Complete `seasonal_difference(x, period)`.

widget.starter:
import numpy as np

def seasonal_difference(x, period):
    x = np.asarray(x, dtype=float)
    return ...                          # today minus the same day one period ago
widget.solution:
import numpy as np

def seasonal_difference(x, period):
    x = np.asarray(x, dtype=float)
    return x[period:] - x[:-period]     # today minus the same day one period ago
widget.how: Check runs 6 hidden tests on short lists and on `make_volume(seed)`, already defined, rounded to 6 places. The first run loads NumPy, which takes a few seconds.

hints.text: It is the lag-1 difference with the lag set to `period`.
Monday is compared with last Monday, five trading days earlier.
`return x[period:] - x[:-period]`.

feedback.correct: Correct. The weekly pattern cancels and the result centres on 0.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Subtract the value `period` days earlier: `x[period:] - x[:-period]`.

explain.text: Each day's weekday effect appears in both terms and cancels, so the seasonal difference has the same mean on every weekday. It costs one period of data at the start. A desk often prefers volume over its average for that weekday, a ratio that keeps the level.

screens.title: When not to difference
screens.prose: Top: the stationary AR(1) with $\phi = 0.5$ from the third screen, differenced anyway. Its neighbouring changes now correlate at −0.28. Bottom: last lesson's spread with one break, differenced.
screens.question: Select all that apply.

options.text: Differencing a stationary series adds a negative lag-1 correlation and throws away its level, which was already modellable
Differencing the spread hides its break among the ordinary daily changes
Differencing is harmless, so it is safe to do by default
options.why: You differenced by reflex. The AR(1)'s changes now correlate at −0.28, and its pull to 0 is gone.

options.text: Differencing fixes the break
options.why: The changes look stationary, but the level shift is still real: day 250's change is 1.64, smaller than many ordinary days. A model of the changes will miss it entirely.

hints.text: Is the first series stationary before differencing?
Look at day 250 in the bottom panel.
The AR(1) was I(0): $d = 0$. The break becomes one change of 1.64 on day 250, lost among the others.

feedback.correct: Correct. $d = 0$ means leave it alone, and a break needs to be modelled, not differenced.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check each statement against what the panels show.

byKey.always: You differenced a stationary series. Neighbouring changes share a shock with opposite signs, and the level it reverts to is lost.

explain.text: For a series that is already I(0), the right $d$ is 0: differencing adds a spurious negative correlation and loses the level. A break turns into a single change in the differences, here no larger than an ordinary day's, so it is easy to miss. Test first, then difference only as often as the test says.

screens.title: The rules
screens.prose: You differenced until the ADF test rejected: $$\Delta^d x_t \text{ stationary} \;\Rightarrow\; x_t \sim \text{I}(d).$$ A stochastic trend (a walk) needs differencing; a deterministic trend needs detrending; the test with a trend term decides. For prices, $\Delta \ln p_t = r_t$: log then difference gives lesson 1's returns. The cost: a return forgets the level (Financial ML, lesson 6, keeps some of it).
screens.question: A share's log price is I(1). What is its daily log return?

options.text: I(0): one difference of an I(1) series is stationary
I(1) as well
options.why: Differencing lowers the order by one. The log return is the first difference of an I(1) series.
That would need the log price to be I(3). Differencing reduces $d$, never raises it.

options.text: Trend-stationary, so it should be detrended
options.why: Returns have no trend to remove; their mean is the drift.

feedback.correct: Correct. That is why returns are the base layer for models.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each difference lowers the order of integration by one.

explain.text: $r_t = \ln p_t - \ln p_{t-1}$ is the first difference of an I(1) series, so it is I(0). The ADF test confirmed it in lesson 3, with a statistic of −44.

screens.title: The research base layer
screens.prose: A research team stores daily log returns, not prices, as the base layer every model reads. One researcher builds a pairs signal from two related shares: the spread $s_t = \ln p^A_t - \beta \ln p^B_t$. Its ADF test rejects a unit root at 1%.
screens.question: Should the spread be differenced before modelling?

options.text: No: it is already I(0), and its level, the distance from its mean, is the signal
Yes: everything in the pipeline is differenced
options.why: You applied the base-layer rule to a stationary series. Differencing the spread throws away the very distance from the mean you want to trade.

options.text: Detrend it first, then difference
options.why: It has no trend and it already rejects a unit root. Either step would only add noise.

options.text: Rebuild it from prices and test those
options.why: The prices are I(1); the point of the spread is that a combination of them is I(0).

hints.text: What did the ADF test say about the spread?
It keeps returning to its mean.
A spread that rejects a unit root is I(0): $d = 0$, so no differencing.

feedback.correct: Correct. A stationary spread is modelled in levels.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use the test result: what $d$ does the spread need?

byKey.yes: You differenced a stationary spread. Its level is the signal: how far it is from where it returns.

explain.text: Two I(1) prices whose combination is I(0) are **cointegrated**, the subject of the Cointegration course later in this topic. That spread is the one level we keep undifferenced. Its distance from the mean is what a pairs trade bets on.

ideas: Differencing a walk returns its shocks; a walk with drift becomes noise around the drift. A series needing $d$ differences is I($d$); log prices are I(1) and returns I(0).
Difference a stochastic trend; detrend a deterministic one. The ADF test with a trend term decides. Detrending a walk leaves a unit root; differencing a straight trend doubles the noise.
Do not difference a stationary series ($d = 0$), and watch for breaks, which differencing hides as one spike. A stationary spread is modelled in levels.

formula.name: Differences
formula.tex: \Delta x_t = x_t - x_{t-1}, \qquad \Delta^2 x_t = \Delta x_t - \Delta x_{t-1}, \qquad \Delta_5 x_t = x_t - x_{t-5}

summary.trap: Fitting a line to a random walk does not remove its trend: the residual still has a unit root.

quiz.prose: A random walk with drift: $x_t = x_{t-1} + 0.2 + \varepsilon_t$ with $\varepsilon_t$ of sd 1.
quiz.question: What is the mean of $\Delta x_t$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write out $x_t - x_{t-1}$.

byKey.zero: You dropped the drift. It survives differencing as the mean of the changes.
byKey.one: You gave the sd of the shock. The mean of the changes is the drift.

explain.text: $\Delta x_t = 0.2 + \varepsilon_t$, so its mean is 0.2 and its sd is 1: noise around a constant.

quiz.prose: An analyst differences daily log prices twice "to be safe".
quiz.question: What is the result?

options.text: Over-differenced returns: stationary, but noisier, with a lag-1 correlation near −0.5
A safer series: twice-differenced data are more stationary still
options.why: Once is enough for an I(1) series. The second difference adds a shock and a spurious negative correlation.

options.text: The same as the returns, since a second difference changes little
options.why: The second difference is the change in returns, $r_t - r_{t-1}$, a different and noisier series.

options.text: A series with a trend, left by the second difference
options.why: Differencing never adds a trend.

feedback.correct: Correct. Difference as often as the test says, and no more.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. What is the difference of a series that is already stationary?

explain.text: $\Delta r_t = r_t - r_{t-1}$: twice the variance of returns and a lag-1 correlation of about −0.5. That pattern is a sign of over-differencing.

quiz.prose: A series has ADF p = 0.001 in levels.
quiz.question: What is the right $d$?

options.text: $d = 0$: it is already stationary

options.why: The level already rejects a unit root. Differencing would only add noise.
Only a series whose first difference still has a unit root needs two.

options.text: Cannot tell without differencing
options.why: The level test answers it: p = 0.001 rejects a unit root.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the test on the levels first.

explain.text: The smallest $d$ whose differenced series rejects a unit root is the order of integration. Here the levels already reject, so $d = 0$.
